extracted.intended_audience: federal judges, court staff, and litigation practitioners managing patent cases
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for judicial management of patent litigation, including when to stay, transfer, or consolidate co-pending proceedings; handling PTO post-grant reviews; jurisdiction, venue, and presuit investigation standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors for stays of co-pending district court proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts typically consider whether (1) a stay would cause undue prejudice to the nonmoving party; (2) a stay will simplify the issues for trial; and (3) discovery is complete and a trial date is set.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These factors parallel those for transfer of venue. The public policy favoring expeditious resolution weighs heavily when patents are wasting assets. When two actions are nearly identical, the first-filed case generally takes priority and the later-filed suit should be dismissed, transferred, or stayed; however, the first-to-file rule is not rigid and exceptions exist for considerations of judicial and litigant economy. Courts should weigh specific prejudice to the nonmovant, potential for simplification of issues, and the stage of litigation on a case-by-case, fact-intensive basis.

rubrics_metrics.name: First-to-file presumption in co-pending patent actions
rubrics_metrics.description: When two actions that sufficiently overlap are filed in different federal district courts, the earlier-filed case generally takes precedence; the later-filed declaratory judgment action is ordinarily stayed, dismissed, or transferred to the forum of the infringement action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rule is a doctrine of federal comity intended to avoid conflicting decisions and promote judicial efficiency. It is applied with discretion; exceptions are available for considerations of judicial and litigant economy or other factors making another forum preferable (e.g., customer-suit exception). The presumption may be rebutted by showing factors such as status of co-pending case, imminent trial, or other equities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Additional factors courts weigh when deciding stays or transfers among co-pending cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts have looked to: status of the co-pending case (e.g., likelihood of dismissal), harm caused by delay, whether the other forum lacks jurisdiction over necessary parties, possibility of consolidation, convenience of the parties, and judicial economy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include considering whether the first-filed case might be dismissed for improper venue, whether delaying the stayed issues will cause harm, feasibility of consolidating proceedings to ensure consistent claim construction, and the relative convenience of forums. Courts are often reluctant to wade into competing stay requests filed in multiple districts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Customer-suit situations and stays
rubrics_metrics.description: Stays of co-pending litigation against customers (customers of the accused technology) are commonly granted when resolution of a supplier/provider suit will resolve liability as to the customer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Based on cases like Katz and Codex, courts sometimes prefer staying customer suits because resolving liability with respect to the supplier may resolve or narrow claims against the customer. Such situations are often treated differently from other co-pendency scenarios.

rubrics_metrics.name: District court discretion to stay litigation pending PTO reexamination/reissue
rubrics_metrics.description: District courts have wide discretion to stay litigation pending Patent Office review (reexamination, reissue), considering similar factors: undue prejudice/tactical disadvantage, simplification of issues, and stage of discovery/trial date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stays were less common pre-AIA due to concerns about PTO timeliness and estoppel effects, but AIA reforms (IPR, PGR, CBM) expedited administrative review and increased stays. Stays are less appropriate when PTO proceedings are initiated late in the litigation. A court cannot condition a stay by directing a party to file PTO proceedings or impose conditions exceeding its case-management powers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-factor test applied to stays pending AIA reviews (IPR/CBM/PGR)
rubrics_metrics.description: Most courts continue to evaluate stay motions according to the three-factor test: (1) undue prejudice to the nonmoving party; (2) whether a stay will simplify issues and trial; (3) whether discovery is complete and a trial date is set.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The inquiry is based on the totality of the circumstances and is not limited to these three factors. Because the PTAB has up to six months to decide whether to institute review and the scope is unknown until institution, many courts are reluctant to grant stays based solely on filing a petition. Courts consider timing, likelihood of institution, and whether PTAB review would resolve the claims before the court; if not, courts may seek stipulations to streamline litigation instead of staying.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing considerations for stays pending PTO/AIA proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: Stays are less appropriate when PTO proceedings are instituted late in the district-court litigation; courts are more likely to stay when PTO review is timely and likely to meaningfully simplify pending litigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include denying stays where PTO petitions have not yet been granted and the stay could result in an unnecessary six-month delay. Conversely, if the case to be stayed is in infancy and the case on which it depends is near trial on invalidity issues or is in a venue with a short time-to-trial, factors may strongly favor a stay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Greater willingness to stay pending Covered Business Method Review (CBMR)
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts have shown greater willingness to stay litigation pending CBMR, recognizing a statutory intent to encourage higher rates of stays for CBMs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some courts add a fourth factor when considering CBMR stays—'whether a stay, or the denial thereof, will reduce the burden of litigation on the parties and on the court'—and have interpreted legislative history as favoring stays. Section 18(b)(2) permits interlocutory appeals from district court stay decisions in CBMR contexts, but the Federal Circuit lacks jurisdiction to hear such appeals until the PTAB institutes CBMR.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of PTAB proceedings on litigation strategy and stay likelihood
rubrics_metrics.description: The AIA-established PTAB procedures (IPR, PGR, CBM) are faster and lower-cost, with high institution and invalidation rates, prompting increased petitions and a higher rate of district-court stays pending PTAB review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statistics through early 2015 showed high institution rates (~80%) and meaningful claim cancellation rates; district courts have stayed litigation pending IPR in a large percentage of cases (rates vary by district and judge). Courts consider potential for PTAB to narrow or cancel claims when evaluating stay motions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 11 presuit investigation standard for filing patent infringement pleadings
rubrics_metrics.description: Rule 11 requires that a party filing a complaint has sufficiently investigated to form a good-faith basis for its claims. A patentee must exercise reasonable diligence to ascertain infringement before filing, including investigation into claim interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patentees are not required to assess validity pre-filing due to patent presumption of validity. The level of inquiry varies by context; where an accused product is readily obtainable, courts expect examination or reasonable explanation for not obtaining a sample. If a patent owner cannot fully investigate (e.g., secret method), Rule 11 permits identifying in pleadings contentions that 'will likely have evidentiary support after a reasonable opportunity for further investigation or discovery' (Fed. R. Civ. P. 11(b)(3)). Failure to investigate (e.g., not obtaining or reverse-engineering an available device) can support unreasonable conduct findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal jurisdiction analysis in patent cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Personal jurisdiction is analyzed in two parts: whether the applicable state long-arm statute is satisfied and whether exercising jurisdiction complies with the Due Process Clause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General jurisdiction follows Daimler's 'essentially at home' standard. For specific jurisdiction, courts commonly rely on stream-of-commerce theories (Asahi plurality split between O'Connor and Brennan tests), and the law remains unsettled. Given uncertainty, the Federal Circuit emphasizes the importance of jurisdictional discovery when the record is inadequate to resolve jurisdictional facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject-matter jurisdiction for patent cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Under 28 U.S.C. § 1338(a), federal district courts have exclusive original jurisdiction of 'any civil action arising under any Act of Congress relating to patents.' Whether a claim arises under patent law is determined from the well-pleaded complaint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases that require resolution of substantive patent law issues (even in state-law causes of action like malpractice) can arise under federal patent law. The determination is made solely on the basis of the complaint, not counterclaims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supplemental jurisdiction over state-law claims in patent disputes
rubrics_metrics.description: District courts may exercise supplemental jurisdiction over state-law claims that form part of the same case or controversy (28 U.S.C. § 1367(a)), but the court has discretionary authority to retain or dismiss such claims under § 1367(c).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If no original federal jurisdiction exists (e.g., lack of standing), supplemental state-law claims must be dismissed. Even after federal claims are dismissed on the merits, courts can choose to retain supplemental state-law claims, based on discretion and applicable considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Venue for patent cases and venue-transfer motions
rubrics_metrics.description: Venue in patent cases is generally governed by 28 U.S.C. § 1391 and permits filing in any district where infringing activity (broadly defined as making, selling, or offering for sale) has occurred; because many products/services are nationwide, plaintiffs often sue in districts where defendants lack physical presence, prompting transfer motions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defendants frequently respond with motions to transfer venue. The Guide discusses transfer practice and related considerations elsewhere (e.g., § 2.3.3.1), and advises courts to weigh convenience, fairness, and statutory factors when ruling on transfer motions.
